title: Are we headed toward recession? Unpredictable. — Harvard Gazette
content: Despite recent “shocks” to the U.S. economy like tariffs, the war with Iran, the spike in fuel and energy prices, and workforce reductions attributed to AI, the country is not in a recession. What signs from history do you look for to help forecast whether one is on the horizon and how detrimental it might be? [...] Why is there always so much fretting currently over the possibility of a recession, given that they tend to be relatively brief and less frequent? It’s especially puzzling since the U.S. notched two of its longest economic expansions ever in the last few decades, and expansions exert greater overall influence on an economy. [...] One of the optimistic findings in the book is that recessions have become less frequent over time in both the U.S. and the U.K. That is a long-run structural trend going all the way back to 1700 with no clear break at any specific points in time toward longer-lived economic expansions.

title: Is the U.S. economy doing better than GDP data suggests? – San Diego Union-Tribune
content:
NO: Headline GDP overstates the economy’s health. AI-related capital spending is contributing roughly half to three-quarters of recent quarterly growth; strip it out and growth is anemic. Consumer spending, normally two-thirds of the economy, has contributed modestly to recent growth; real wage gains have stalled; and job growth is slowing. The economy isn’t in recession, but its apparent strength rests on an unusual tech splurge, along with significant fiscal spending at the expense of added [...] headline probably understates current momentum, but the outlook is increasingly fragile. [...] U.S. economic growth, as measured by the country’s gross domestic product, slowed to 1.5% from April through June, down from 2.1% growth in the first three months of 2026, according to new data from the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis.

The slowing rate of economic output is due, in part, to a downturn in both government spending and exports. Increased imports of telecommunications equipment, semiconductors and related devices also dragged down GDP.

title: U.S. employers unexpectedly cut 23,000 jobs amid strain from the Iran war, unemployment dips to 4.1% | PBS News
content:
Economists have used the term "no hire, no fire'' to describe the unusual job market conditions.

So far this year, employers are adding 61,000 jobs a month, up from 9,700 in 2025, the weakest outside a recession since 2002. [...] Tthe United States doesn't need as many jobs as it used to keep the unemployment rate from rising. Trump's immigration crackdown and the ongoing retirement of baby boomers mean fewer people are competing for work. So the "break-even'' rate of monthly hiring, 155,000 in 2023-2024, has dropped, perhaps to nearly zero, according to a Federal Reserve study. [...] One week in July the number of Americans filing for unemployment benefits dropped to the lowest level in more than 50 years. The jobless rate tumbled to 4.2% in June, the lowest in a year, and is expected to have stayed there last month, according to a survey of forecasters by the data firm FactSet.

But Americans who have lost their jobs – or are seeking to bust into the job market for the first time – are struggling to catch a break.

content: when adjusted for purchasing power, to that of the United States. Today, China is much poorer on a relative basis than Japan was. Its per capita income, when adjusted for purchasing power, is about half of Japan’s and one third of the United States’. China also faces a worse demographic outlook than Japan did and lacks the institutional infrastructure that enabled Tokyo to gradually recover. [...] China now accounts for roughly 30 percent of global industrial production, and by 2030, it is expected to reach 45 percent, according to a 2024 UN report. With the exception of the U.S. economy immediately after World War II, there is no historical precedent for such a concentration of industrial power. Measured as a share of global GDP, China’s current manufactured goods surplus is greater than the combined surpluses of Germany and Japan at any point during the 1980s. [...] To avoid the most catastrophic outcome, China must orchestrate, with the United States and other major economies, a preemptive and gradual rebalancing of its economy. Such a coordinated approach might replicate the spirit of the 1985 Plaza Accord, an agreement between France, Japan, the United States, the United Kingdom, and West Germany to intervene in foreign exchange markets to bring down the highly overvalued U.S. dollar and reduce the large U.S. trade deficit.
